title: Day Bar Clocks
context: Grade 5, the pages on the 24-hour clock. An adult sees a rule for changing clocks. What the pages are doing is making a 24-hour time the hours and minutes since midnight, and making the 12 o'clock hour the hour where the rule of adding 12 does not hold.

writeup.why: Read a 24-hour time as the hours and minutes after midnight, change 12-hour times into 24-hour times by adding 12 from one o'clock on in the afternoon, treat the 12 o'clock hour on its own, and change 24-hour times back into 12-hour times.
writeup.look: One day bar from 12 midnight to 12 midnight with the 24-hour times above and the 12-hour times below, a sliding marker and a violet tile of 12 h.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Day Bar Clocks' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of times converted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The day bar runs across the area along y 420 from x 90 to x 1130, 90 tall, with 12 midnight at the left end and 12 midnight at the right end and 12 noon marked where the halves meet. The 24-hour times stand above it along y 350 and the 12-hour times below it along y 540, all in near-black ink. The half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m., and the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m. The marker slides along the bar, amber while it is being placed. The time the question gives is set in deep blue, labelled Given, on whichever clock it is given on, and the same time is read on the other clock in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 650. A 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours, and a zero that holds the front place open is grey, labelled Place holder. The violet tile of 12 h, labelled Jump, waits at x 900, y 230 and is dragged onto the hour of a p.m. time from one o'clock on. On the third phase the two 12 o'clock hours are lit amber on the bar and the tile will not settle in either. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for a.m., p.m. and hours. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last time stays on the bar with its marker, both clocks read beside it and the tile where it was used.

phases.win: the four digits and the word hours turn green, and the 12-hour time shows beneath
phases.does: slides the marker along the bar, reads the hours and minutes after midnight, and writes them as four digits with a grey zero holding the front place
phases.goal: a 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours: the first two digits are the hours after midnight and the last two are the minutes
phases.says: How many hours after midnight? Then how many minutes?
phases.check: Away from the screen: why does a time just after midnight begin with a zero?
phases.feels: the marker's distance from midnight turning into four digits and the word hours
phases.hands: Stand a paper day bar on a desk and slide a paper marker along it. Read the hours and the minutes after midnight at the marker, and write them as four digits with the word hours.
phases.tries: First rung: read the hours only, with the minutes at nothing. Second rung: add the minutes and write all four digits. Third rung: the same task with a time early in the morning, before the question's own time returns.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the tile is tried on a time in a 12 o'clock hour, it shivers and slides off, the two 12 o'clock hours on the bar glow amber once, and the time is written right without it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet converted. On the first phase the day bar runs from 12 midnight to 12 midnight with the 24-hour times above it and the 12-hour times below, and the marker waits at the left end. On the second the marker sits on a p.m. time and the violet tile of 12 h waits beside the bar. On the third the two 12 o'clock hours stand out on the bar, one just after midnight and one just after noon, with the tile beside them. On the fourth the marker sits on a 24-hour time in deep blue and the 12-hour row waits empty. One thing moves, once: the marker or the tile gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any time set on the day bar and read on either clock, with the tile tried in any hour. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on four digits after midnight, adding 12, the 12 o'clock hour and writing a 24-hour time back on the 12-hour clock.
voiceLines: A day bar, from one midnight to the next.
How many hours after midnight? Then how many minutes?
Is it after one o'clock in the afternoon? Then what do you add to the hour?
The hour that begins at twelve is special. What would adding twelve do here?
Is it before noon or after? What do you do to the hours?
A new time on the bar. Read it on the other clock.
Free play. Slide the marker anywhere and read it on both clocks.
Look at the bar again. Which half of the day is the marker in?
You read one time on both clocks and kept the twelve o'clock hour apart.

observations.why: a time on either clock is the hours and minutes after midnight.
observations.soWhat: read a 24-hour time as the hours and minutes after midnight, in four digits and the word hours.
observations.observe: The marker was the same distance from the left end of the bar whichever clock the time was read on.

observations.why: an afternoon hour from one o'clock on has 12 h more before it than the same hour in the morning.
observations.soWhat: add 12 to a p.m. hour from one o'clock on, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and keep the minutes.
observations.observe: The tile of 12 h fitted onto the hour of an afternoon time and made it the hour of a 24-hour time.

observations.why: 12:40 a.m. is 40 min after midnight, and 12:40 p.m. is 12 h 40 min after midnight.
observations.soWhat: the hour that begins at 12 is a case of its own on both clocks, so the tile is kept off it.
observations.observe: The tile would not settle in either 12 o'clock hour.

observations.why: from 1300 hours on the hours are 13 or more, so 12 has been added, and before 1200 hours it is still the morning.
observations.soWhat: take away 12 from the hours from 1300 hours on, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and write a.m. or p.m. after the time.
observations.observe: Going back, the tile came off only from 1300 hours on, and a time before 1200 hours was called a.m.

description: Slide a time along one day bar and read it on the 12-hour clock and the 24-hour clock, add 12 to a p.m. hour except in the 12 o'clock hour, and see why that hour is a case of its own.

source_tool.description: One day bar fills the working area from 12 midnight on the left to 12 midnight on the right, with two rows of times along it: the 24-hour times above and the 12-hour times below. The half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m., and the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., with 12 noon marked where they meet. A marker slides along the bar. The time the question gives is set on it in deep blue, labelled Given, on one of the two clocks, and the same time is read on the other clock in green, labelled Answer. A 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours, and a zero that holds the front place open is grey, labelled Place holder. On the second phase a violet tile of 12 h, labelled Jump, is dragged onto the hour of a p.m. time from one o'clock on and adds 12 to it. On the third phase the two 12 o'clock hours are lit amber on the bar, one just after midnight and one just after noon, and the tile will not fit in either. On the fourth phase the tile is taken off from 1300 hours on, and a time before 1200 hours is given a.m. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the times converted.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the bar again. Which half of the day is the marker in?
voice.onNext: A new time on the bar. Read it on the other clock.
voice.opening: A day bar, from one midnight to the next.
voice.onFinish: You read one time on both clocks and kept the twelve o'clock hour apart.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Slide the marker anywhere and read it on both clocks.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has read a station board written in 24-hour time beside a wall clock, and has said what the four digits are. The tool is what lines the two clocks up on one bar, the 12 o'clock hours included, which a table of matching times only lists.

answer_key.rule: A 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours: the first two digits are the hours after midnight and the last two are the minutes. For a p.m. time from one o'clock on, add 12 to the hour, except in the 12 o'clock hour. 12:40 a.m. is 0040 hours, 12 noon is 1200 hours and 12:40 p.m. is 1240 hours, and 12 midnight is 0000 hours. Going back, from 1300 hours on take away 12 from the hours, except in the 12 o'clock hour. A time before 1200 hours is a.m., and 0020 hours is 12:20 a.m. Noon and midnight are written 12 noon and 12 midnight, never with a.m. or p.m.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the time as the child wrote it. A p.m. time from one o'clock on written with no 12 added stays, and the tile it is missing is lit amber. A 12 o'clock hour time that has had 12 added shows a time past 2359 hours, which is no time, and the 12 o'clock hour is lit amber on the bar. A 24-hour time with its front zero left off stays, and the empty place is lit grey. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A 24-hour time has four digits and the word hours.
The first two digits are the hours after midnight, and the last two are the minutes.
So 0925 hours is 9 h 25 min after midnight.
9 h 25 min after midnight is before noon, so it is 9:25 a.m.
items.answer: 9 h 25 min after midnight, so it is 9:25 a.m.
items.question: A ferry timetable shows 0925 hours. How long after midnight is that, and is it morning or evening?
items.checkpoint: A 24-hour time is the hours and minutes after midnight, in four digits.
items.misconception: Reading the first two digits as the minutes and the last two as the hours.

steps: For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour, except in the 12 o'clock hour.
The hour is 6, not 12, so the rule holds: 6 + 12 = 18.
The minutes stay as they are, so write 18 and 20 together.
items.question: What is 6:20 p.m. on the 24-hour clock?
items.checkpoint: For a p.m. time, add 12 to the hour and keep the minutes, except in the 12 o'clock hour.
items.misconception: Adding 12 to the minutes instead of the hours.

steps: The 12 o'clock hour is a case of its own, so do not add 12 to it.
12:35 a.m. is 35 min after midnight, so it is written 0035 hours.
12:35 p.m. keeps its 12 after noon, so it is written 1235 hours.
So 12:35 a.m. is 0035 hours, and 12:35 p.m. is 1235 hours.
items.answer: 0035 hours for 12:35 a.m., and 1235 hours for 12:35 p.m.
items.question: What is 12:35 a.m. on the 24-hour clock, and what is 12:35 p.m.?
items.checkpoint: In the 12 o'clock hour do not add 12: after midnight the hour is 00, and after noon it stays 12.
items.misconception: Adding 12 to the 12 o'clock hour after noon, which gives a time past 2359 hours, and that is no time.

steps: 2245 hours is after 1300 hours, so take away 12 from the hours.
22 - 12 = 10, so the hour is 10 and the minutes are 45.
It is after noon, so write p.m. after the time.
items.question: What is 2245 hours on the 12-hour clock?
items.checkpoint: From 1300 hours on, take away 12 from the hours, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and write p.m.
items.misconception: Taking away 12 but leaving off p.m., so the time could be morning or evening.

teaching_notes: Read a 24-hour time as the hours and minutes after midnight, and say it that way: 0925 hours is 9 h 25 min after midnight. Add 12 to a p.m. hour, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and take 12 away only from 1300 hours on, except in the 12 o'clock hour. Teach the 12 o'clock hour on both clocks separately: 12:40 a.m. is 0040 hours and 12:40 p.m. is 1240 hours. Write noon and midnight in words, 12 noon and 12 midnight, never with a.m. or p.m. Write a 24-hour time as four digits and the word hours, with no colon and no dot, and never name an hour by its order.
generation_prompt: Build a clock conversion tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. One day bar runs from 12 midnight to 12 midnight with 24-hour times above it and 12-hour times below. The half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside an outline, labelled a.m., and the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., with 12 noon marked between. A marker slides along the bar; the given time is deep blue, labelled Given, and the same time on the other clock is green, labelled Answer. A 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours, with a grey zero, labelled Place holder, holding the front place. A violet tile of 12 h, labelled Jump, is dragged onto a p.m. hour to add 12, except in either 12 o'clock hour, where it will not fit and the hour is lit amber. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Slide the marker along the day bar. Read the time on the other clock, add or take away the 12 h tile where the rule says, and look at the 12 o'clock hours twice.
